members.text: Master your senses, passion, lust and anger, overcome ignorance and sloth, and seek lasting inner contentment over sensual pleasure.
Do not treat pleasure as good; keep your mind undisturbed by bodily pleasure and pain without adding opinions of good or bad to sensations.
Rulers should lead by their own correct, serious, consistent example, be humble, free of greed and fond of propriety and good faith, and avoid killing.
Serve your ruler according to what is right and with faithfulness, retire if you cannot, and still take office; hide your wisdom in disorder.
Rulers, like true physicians and pilots, should consider the interest of their subjects, not their own.
Rulers should love their own parents and be polite to elders so that the people follow the example.
Serve your sovereign with utmost loyalty, repair his wrongs, carry out his good schemes, and correct his faults.
Rulers should not forget sound policy and should cherish subjects in word, thought, and deed.
Rulers should practice righteousness, avoid avarice and lust, and remove traitors from the palace.
Take responsibility for your problems, even those not your fault.
Understand that all problems are interpersonal relationship problems.
In relationships, work through problems rather than blaming partners' traits.
Learn to serve people and understand life before serving spirits or understanding death, do not sacrifice to spirits not your own, and do not offend the highest power.
Remember death is near: do good during life, avoid pride, be ready to leave without a murmur, and expect to answer for your conduct.
Remember you will die, to clarify what matters.

Seek realization of your identity with the ultimate reality, since liberation comes by no other means.
Hold firm to your resolve for liberation and follow the prescribed rule, never returning to worldly life.

Strengthen discrimination and renunciation first, and carefully purify the mind.
Attend first to the culture of the mind; cleaning the mind is the essence of religion.
Treat relatives, great ministers and old families fairly, do not demand all talents of one man, and keep a grave, sincere manner in high station.
Do not do to others what you do not want done to yourself.
Love and know all people, honor the talented and virtuous, bear with all, pity the incompetent, give rest to the aged, treat the young tenderly, and perfect others' good qualities.
Judge people by their conduct and examination, not by words, appearances or popular opinion alone, and do not praise or blame beyond what is proper.
Be forbearing in small matters and do not dwell on, blame or remember others' past wrongs; receive people who come to you in good faith.
Be sincere and truthful, make righteousness the core of everything, do what you see is right, and carry out in conduct what you profess.
Do not put on a false appearance: avoid pretended firmness, flattery, fine words, hidden resentment, false uprightness, pleasing everyone, and pretending to have what you lack.
Love virtue more than beauty, wealth or reputation, pursue good tirelessly, find joy in simple living, and think of righteousness when gain is offered.
Be ready to sacrifice your life rather than injure virtue or when danger threatens, and take up virtue as a burden carried until death.
Keep to the due mean: avoid excess and deficiency, keep latitude only in small virtues, be sparing in ceremony, and restrain over-haste.
Make friends of the virtuous, serve under worthy officers, meet friends on grounds of culture, admonish friends faithfully but stop if hopeless, and keep respect for old friends.
Speak to those who can be spoken with, avoid idle talk and hearsay, and use words correctly so that what you say can be carried out.
Be dignified without wrangling and sociable without faction, avoid contention, stay flexible with no fixed course for or against, and match advice to temperament.
Bear sorrow and joy, heat and cold, praise and blame with strong, constant calm, regarding friend and foe alike.
Cultivate fearlessness, charity, tenderness, patience, purity and truthfulness, and harm no living thing, free of wrath, revenge, pride and arrogance.
Do your duty without attachment or desire for the results, giving up the fruit of action and staying calm in success and failure.
Do your own appointed work diligently, even if flawed, rather than another's work done well, and never abandon your natural duty.
Keep working rightly rather than ceasing from action; do not abstain from work that keeps the world turning.
Act to uphold others and set an example, and let the enlightened work without unsettling the untaught.
Avoid lust, anger, greed, arrogance, spite, envy and jealousy, and give up pride of caste, family and station.
Do not value fame or repute, do not seek posthumous praise, and do not rank others' opinion of you above your own.
Do not be angry at wrongdoers: expect wrongdoing, remember you err likewise and that all will soon be dead, and be benevolent even to the unjust.
Correct wrongdoers by showing them their error if they are willing to listen; otherwise be indulgent toward them.
Be just, truthful and modest in word and deed, do what is due, and do not do wrong, since the wrongdoer harms himself.
Be good today and do not delay; act as if each act were your last, with dignity, simplicity and no regret.
Regard yourself as part of a human community governed by common reason; direct your actions to the common good and do only what is necessary.
Cooperate with others, love those among whom you live sincerely, attend to what they say, and do not turn away from them in vexation.
Do not look at what your neighbor says or does; look only to making your own acts just and pure, and examine others' guiding principles.
Keep your principles ready at hand like a fighter who never drops his guard, and persevere until you have made them your own.
Follow truth always, hate a lie, and keep striving to grasp the real nature of each essence rather than resting in appearances.
Trust measuring, numbering and weighing over appearances, let the rational part of the soul govern, and do not rely on analogy alone.
Ridicule only folly and vice, weigh the beautiful by the standard of the good, and prefer things uncovered to covered up.
Do not act haughtily, be frugal, and do not be insolent to the lowly or proud of high position.
Do not show dissatisfaction with a position lower than that of others.
Be truthful and real in substance, not merely seeming; make sure being right also looks right.
Avoid familiarity, boring others, and being importunate; be brief, sparing with your presence, and use absence to be more esteemed.
Do not parade or enforce the dignity of your position; create respect and be valued for your talents.
Read people: find their ruling passion, test their character by deeds, watch those who act on second thoughts, and do not be fooled by flattery.
Stay independent: keep resources double, avoid being responsible for everyone, and do not let any single vote or fashion decide your worth.
Seek the approval of wise and distinguished people rather than the mob, and keep steady under both criticism and applause.
Cultivate a good manner and keep the favour of the mighty; aim to be loved with respect rather than passion.
Ignore slander and the talk of the vulgar, and know vulgarity in order to avoid it.
Tell the truth and keep your word; do not lie or make promises you cannot keep.
Avoid the vile and low-minded and do not serve senseless princes or beg from misers.
Judge people by virtue, understanding, and intrinsic value, not by birth or outward appearance.
Speak discreetly and respectfully to everyone, listen to all without anger, examine what is said, and do not shun others as unclean.
Injure no one, avoid covetousness and the worst sins, and do not covet others' wealth.
Love other people for your own good, not to please God.
Care only about what truly matters, and choose your values carefully.
Treat yourself like someone you are responsible for helping, caring for your own health and future as you would for another.
Avoid resentment, deceit, and arrogance, which lead toward cruelty and hell on earth.
Do not seek recognition or approval from others; living for others' expectations means living their life.
Neither praise nor rebuke others; instead offer encouragement and express gratitude.
Have confidence in others unconditionally, trusting them without demanding collateral.
Do not view interpersonal relations as competitions; others' happiness is not your defeat.

Haughtiness and insolence toward inferiors.
Trusting one resource; making many dependent on you; living wholly for oneself or others; dying of another's ill-luck.
Vanity, delusion, covetousness, wrangling, and hypocrisy.
Associating with the vile, serving senseless rulers, begging from misers.
Disobeying parents, despising an elder brother, abandoning brothers, departing from custom.
Ignorance, delusion, falling into sin despite understanding.
Covetousness, embezzling alms, harming others.
Selfishness; sinful acts.
Group-bound morality, stratified classes, privilege for a few, exclusive morality among thieves, businessmen, and castes.
Promote upright, virtuous and talented people to office and set aside the crooked; do not hide worthy people you know.
Make morality sacred and universal, with common rules and brotherhood effective for all, not bound to one group.
Love learning and pursue it eagerly, even if you are dull or naturally active, and pair every virtue with a love of learning.
Learn widely, seek the one principle behind it, inquire earnestly, ask even your inferiors, take others as teachers, reflect, and put learning to practical use.
Study the old poetry and the rules of propriety to arouse the mind, establish character and finish the self.
Seek true knowledge with reverence and humble inquiry of teachers, cut doubt with wisdom, and cultivate an intellect that knows what to do and avoid.
Do not over-study, dispute, or learn only abstruse subjects; practice what you learn instead of reading alone.
Abide in heedfulness, be earnest in effort to become free from sensuality, delusion, and ignorance, and know the right time to visit a teacher.
Gain knowledge or surround yourself with those who have it, seek counsel, choose and test good assistants, and join knowledge with good intentions.
Ask for help and accept it, rather than only offering it.
Keep traditional ceremonies and show respect and sincere reverence in rites, mourning and sacrifice, without usurping ceremonies above your station, and place humaneness before rites.
Remember your ancestors, keep cultivating the virtue you inherit, never dishonor them, and offer them sacrifices.
Keep the customary ablutions and morning devotions, and honor priests, gods, teacher, and parents even when already pure.
Stay true to your own religion and revile no other creed, avoiding forbidden practices.
Do not practice prayers, pilgrimages, rituals, ceremonies, or sacrifices; real religion lies in observing its tenets, not in books.
Drain the shallows: schedule every minute of your workday and limit shallow work.
Use a shutdown ritual to end work fully each day.
Set a fixed end time for work and plan backward from it.
Shorten deadlines because work expands to fill the time available.
Help others out of trouble without any motive, as the good and magnanimous do.
Contribute to others, since feeling useful to others gives a sense of worth.
Feel worth by simply existing, recognizing that one's being alone contributes to others.
Use implementation intentions, specifying when and where you will act.
Use the do-something principle: action creates motivation.
If you cannot fix your mind on the deity, do not despair: fall back to lower service and works pleasing to it, then to giving up the fruits of labor.
Fix your mind and heart on the deity alone, who dwells within you, and call on him as your helper.
Do not rely on praying to gods to reach union with a creator; practice the qualities that make a true priest.
Embrace failure as part of growth.
See failure as an opportunity to learn, not a judgment of worth.
Embrace challenges rather than avoiding them.
Find inspiration in others' success rather than feeling threatened.
Avoid the paradox of success, where success leads to distraction.
Set your own house in perfect order before criticizing the world.
Do not let family members see what you discard, and do not foist unwanted things on them.
Tidy your own things rather than others' belongings; let family tidy their own.
Greet your house when you come home and treat your belongings with respect.
Empty your bag every day when you get home.
Frequently consider the connection of all things and your small place in the whole, and act in accord with that nature.
Live earnestly in the here and now, treating life as a series of moments like a dance.
Understand that almost everything is nonessential; only a few things matter.
Focus on the present moment and what's important now.
Do not cling to unreal things or the dream-world of appearances, and keep your thoughts on the Self.
Accept yourself as you are, distinguishing what you can change from what you cannot.
Pursue what is meaningful, not what is expedient, even when it demands sacrifice.
Pursue less but better: focus only on what is essential.
Accept trade-offs rather than trying to do everything.

Have faith and do not doubt, receive the teaching with faith, and meditate on it before acting as you choose.
Share the teaching only among faithful devotees, not with those who lack faith or mock, and read or hear it piously.
Abide in faith, devotion and meditation, never be careless in your steadfastness, and carefully concentrate the mind.
Do not get lost in scripture or repeating a word; seek direct realization of the Self.
Know yourself before instructing others, seek a teacher, and as a teacher guide disciples to holiness.

Remember that outside things cannot touch the soul; disturbance and the sense of harm come only from your own opinion, so drop the opinion.
Be wary of imitative art and poetry that appeals to the passionate, irrational part of the soul.
Worship the deity with single, whole-hearted faith, make it your supreme joy and refuge, and keep your heart and mind fixed on it always.
Do everything, including eating, giving and praying, for the deity, as its own, offering even simple gifts in faith and love.
At the hour of death, meditate on the deity alone, shutting the senses and fixing breath and thought on it.
Worship the deity alone, with no other gods, and do not rely on rituals, gifts, penance or sacrifice for rewards in paradise.
Accept with contentment whatever happens in the order of nature, receive it as given, and follow it willingly.
Reverence the deity, be thankful for the good in your life, do not dispute the order of things, and wait for your end in tranquility doing good.
Always represent the deity as truly good, never as the cause of evil nor as changing shape or disguising itself.
Love the deity and stay constant in devotion to him, going about your tasks with your heart fixed on him.
Pray to and meditate on the deity in faith, valuing faith above other virtues; without prayer salvation is not possible.
Worship the compassionate deity wholeheartedly, discard vanity and delusion, and cease wrangling and hypocrisy.
Do not oppose the deity or hope to prosper while doing so.
Hear or recite the tale of the deity's deeds devoutly, with love and reverence.
Practise penance as the only means of approach to the deity and escape from sorrow.
Recognize the truth about the deity without doubt and submit to the commands of God.
Seek wisdom and knowledge of the deity and of yourself; use discrimination to end ignorance, delusion, and grief.

Be grateful for good done to you and forget sinful connections and others' faults; do not grieve a friend.

Endure poverty with composure and contentment rather than distress, and do not place yourself in a low, disreputable position.
Treat prosperity and adversity alike, neither triumphing in the one nor being downcast in the other.
Give generously to the poor and needy, especially food, often and with kindness, rather than only advising others to give.
Do not hoard or bury wealth, or treat possessions as your own; use it or give it away, since you cannot take it with you.
Do not rely on divination or astrology; accept what is destined, and be patient in poverty without grieving over lack of wealth.
Cultivate a sense of worthiness and 'enough' instead of a culture of scarcity.
Practice relative wealth thinking—value what money enables.
Learn from a knower of the truth, listen attentively, then reflect and meditate yourself, deciding for yourself what is Self and not-Self.
Find the truth for yourself rather than relying on others' belief or uncertain tradition, and accept only what trustworthy people free of faults have said.
Even when unsure of the truth, set your mind on the good.
Be uncertain about your beliefs and willing to be wrong.

Seek realization of your identity with the ultimate reality, since liberation comes by no other means.
See the entire universe as nothing but the one reality, and not as separate from it.

Be satisfied with the bliss of the Self and live happily in it, drinking joyfully of it with senses restrained.

Treat family ties and the perishable body as unreal; do not labor for wealth for family or dote on the body.

Do not escape from the world or practice asceticism; change the world and make it better.
Reject fatalism, including predestination by a God and the view that past deeds make present activity impotent.
Use a guiding star of contributing to others to orient your freedom.

Do not let your ruling part be a puppet pulled by fear, desire or suspicion; whirling passions are weaker than the divine thing in you.
